findings.title: Detach asynchronous writes from request cancellation
findings.body: All four asynchronous write paths derive their timeout context from the incoming request context. HTTP request contexts are canceled when the handler returns, and WithTimeoutCause does not remove that parent cancellation. Consequently, a successful unified-storage write can be followed by a canceled legacy write as soon as the response is sent, rather than receiving the intended ten-second window. Preserve request values while detaching cancellation, for example with context.WithoutCancel, before applying the background-write timeout.

findings.title: Preserve mutation order in asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: Each successful mutation launches an independent goroutine, so legacy writes can execute out of order even for sequential client requests. For example, a client can successfully create an object and then delete it while the legacy create is delayed. The legacy delete can see NotFound before the create finishes, leaving the deleted object present in legacy storage indefinitely. The timeout does not prevent this. Mirror operations need ordering per object, or another mechanism that preserves unified-storage commit order.

findings.title: Mirror the committed update instead of replaying UpdatedObjectInfo
findings.body: UpdatedObjectInfo can calculate a patch from the existing object. Passing the original callback to Legacy.Update evaluates that patch against legacy state rather than copying the result committed by Storage.Update. If legacy is behind after a failed mirror write, a patch changing only the title can retain stale interval or item values in legacy even though unified storage contains the correct values. The removed updateWrapper previously supplied the committed result to legacy. Restore that behavior so the mirror receives the accepted object rather than independently replaying the client update.

findings.title: Do not use object names as duration-metric label values
findings.body: The successful delete path passes name to recordStorageDuration where the other paths pass options.Kind. This produces a distinct metric label value for every deleted object rather than a bounded value per kind, and successful and failed deletes use different labeling conventions. Prometheus retains those series, so continued creation and deletion of uniquely named objects causes growing metric cardinality and memory/scrape costs. Pass the kind consistently.

findings.title: Attribute duration and error metrics to the backend actually called
findings.body: The Storage.Create error branch records a legacy duration even though legacy was never called; Storage.Update has the same error at line 129. Conversely, the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection call records a storage duration at line 166. Unified create/update failures therefore disappear from unified-storage error metrics, while legacy collection deletes add extra unified-storage samples and never appear in legacy metrics. Use recordStorageDuration for primary calls and recordLegacyDuration for mirror calls.

findings.title: Use independent backend mocks and assert asynchronous calls
findings.body: The new tests give legacy and unified storage the same mock.Mock, so an expectation configured for either backend satisfies calls to both. For example, the create failure case configures only setupLegacyFn, yet that expectation also supplies the unified-storage failure. The tests also neither wait for nor assert the asynchronous mirror calls. They can therefore pass when reads use the wrong backend or legacy writes are omitted entirely. Use separate mocks, explicit call expectations, and synchronization to verify the asynchronous writes before each test finishes.
